steps.observation: You have 60 seconds. Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
The foghorn had been silent for three days when Elias heard the knocking.

He stood at the kitchen sink of the lighthouse, hands in cold dishwater, listening. It came again: three slow knocks from the heavy oak door below, each one quietly certain, like someone who had been here before and expected to be let in.

No one came to North Ravelin Light anymore. The sea lanes had shifted years ago; ships passed twenty miles to the east, guided by satellites and screens that could see through any fog. The lighthouse had been automated, then decommissioned. Only Elias had refused to go.

He dried his hands on his shirt and descended the spiral steps, the stone curved smooth from a hundred years of climbing boots. The lantern room above him ticked and settled in the cooling evening; the great glass lens, unlit now, kept its own slow vigil with the sky.

At the bottom, he hesitated. The knocking had stopped. Wind moved through the keyhole with a thin, whistling breath.

“Who’s there?” he called.

Silence. Then, very faintly, the sound of waves, though he knew the tide was far out and the rocks below lay bare.

Elias lifted the latch.

Nobody stood on the threshold. The iron catwalk that circled the lighthouse was empty, the low stone wall beyond it bearded with lichen and pale in the mist. But the world smelled wrong. Not like salt and kelp and engine oil, but like rain on hot pavement, like summer storms over a city street.

He saw the envelope at his feet.

It was dry despite the fog, the paper a pale yellow gone soft with age. His name was written on it in a hand he recognized at once: his own, the letters way they’d looked decades ago, before the arthritis, before the tremor that made his pen hesitate.

Elias closed the door and turned the key. He took the envelope to the wooden table where he ate his meals and fixed his clocks. The small brass alarm clock there ticked loudly in the quiet room. He slit the envelope with the edge of a butter knife.

The letter inside was dated forty years past. He remembered it then—not its contents, but its making. The year the storms had been the worst. The year they’d said the light wouldn’t be needed much longer.

Write something for yourself, the visiting teacher had said, leaving paper and pens with the keepers’ children. Something you want to remember when you’re old.

He had been nineteen and scornful of the mainland and its teachers, but he had written anyway, here at this same table. He had sealed the letter and given it to her, annoyed and a little embarrassed. She had promised to post it on to a government scheme: letters to the future, delivered in thirty years. No one had believed they’d really bother.

They never had, he thought. Not until now.

His fingers shook as he unfolded the paper. The ink had browned, but the lines were clear.

If I am still here when this finds me, it began, I hope I have not forgotten why.

He read.

You think you’re going to leave, I know you do. You say it every time the supply boat comes. You look at the captain like he’s already taken your place. But you won’t. You won’t because you know what happens when the light goes out.

You remember the wreck of the Hildegard when you were eleven. You watched the sea take the ship apart on the reef, watched the flare go up red and useless in the storm. You watched men in yellow slickers pull white sheets over faces on the jetty. You saw your father’s back as he looked at the dead and did not turn around.

When the mechanic from the city came last month, he told you the computers were better. That the light was “legacy infrastructure.” He laughed when you said the sea doesn’t care about computers. He said, “Progress doesn’t ask for permission,” and ticked a box on his form. You watched him leave and you knew—no matter what they did, no matter how they wired or coded or measured—you would keep watch as long as you could. Because you have seen what happens in the dark.

If you’re old when you read this, and the others have gone, and the ships have moved away, and they tell you it doesn’t matter anymore: it still matters. Light isn’t for the ships that know where they’re going. It’s for the ones that don’t.

Elias paused, throat tight. The ticking clock sounded suddenly like the lighthouse’s old rotation gear, the slow, patient grind that had marked his childhood nights.

The letter went on, lines he did not remember writing, and yet they were his, younger and almost cruel in their certainty.

You’re afraid of being useless. Of dying here and being found years later by some stranger with a clipboard. You’re afraid that if the light goes out and nothing crashes, they’ll be right about you. That you never mattered as much as you thought.

So listen: you are not here to be proved right by disaster. You are here so that the disaster doesn’t come. That means you never get to know what you’ve prevented. You live your whole life in the maybe. You live with the idea that the world stays ordinary because you refused to let it become otherwise.

That is the work.

The lantern, silent above, seemed to hum in his memory. His father’s hands, cracked and smelling of diesel and salt, guiding his on the winch. The long nights of fog when the beam carved tunnels through the gray and he could hear, but not see, the passage of ships out in the dark.

Elias read to the end.

If there comes a night you can barely climb the stairs and you think, No one will know if I don’t, remember this: somewhere out on that black water is one captain whose radar has gone wrong, one fisherman who left late, one child leaning over a rail. They don’t know you. They’ll never thank you. But they’re moving toward you all the same.

Light the lamp for them. Even if they never see it.

Your hand is probably shaking. Your knees probably hurt. Climb anyway. Turn the wheel. Let the light go around one more time.

I promise you—it’s enough.

Elias sat for a long time without moving. Outside, dusk had thickened into that close, muffled blue that made the sea and sky one piece. The horizon was gone. The world was just the tower and the fog and the slow heave of unseen water.

Up in the lantern room, the modern beacon—small, efficient, dull—slept in its housing, powered down when they’d cut the funding. But behind it, still bolted to the iron frame, was the great Fresnel lens, its facets dusty but unbroken, catching what little light there was and breaking it into dull rainbows.

His knees did hurt. The climb would be slower than it used to be. The old oil lamp had been removed years ago; there was nothing to light. No reason, they’d said.

He folded the letter carefully and slid it back into its envelope. Then he rose, his chair scraping against the worn floorboards, and set the envelope under the brass clock, where he kept things that must not be lost.

On the wall by the door hung his father’s coat, the oilskin gone stiff with age. He shrugged it on and felt its weight settle around his shoulders, smelled, faintly, tobacco and salt that the years had missed.

The spiral steps took him upward, each one a small ache. Halfway, he had to pause, hand against the stone, breath short. He could hear the sea more clearly here, the boom and hiss of it against the rocks below.

No one will know if I don’t, the present thought whispered.

He climbed.

In the lantern room, everything was as he had left it the day the officials had come with their forms and their polite finality. The metal instruments, unplugged. The cables, coiled. The lens, patient.

Elias crossed to the breaker box. The wires from the mainland were still live; they had not bothered to cut them, only to switch them off.

“You think the computers are better,” his younger hand had written. “You think progress doesn’t ask permission.”

He flipped the switches up, one by one.

There was a low, hesitant hum, the kind of sound a machine makes when stirring out of an old sleep. A test pattern of light flickered in the housing of the small modern beacon. For a moment, Elias thought that would be all—a feeble glow, a token.

Then the room filled with radiance.

The great lens gathered and focused the light, took that small obedient beam and made of it a long, white spear that shot out into the fog. The tower seemed to straighten, the glass around him glinting like water under starlight.

The beam swept slow and sure across the horizon, the same motion it had traced when his father was young, when ships had lined up along the light’s path like beads on a string.

Elias leaned both hands on the rail and watched it turn. Somewhere out there in the gray, maybe no one saw it. Maybe the satellites were working perfectly. Maybe every captain tonight knew exactly where he was.

Maybe.

As the light moved, something at the edge of the mist glimmered back—a brief, answering flash, low and small, the kind a trawler’s mast lamp might make when its bow lifted over a swell.

He could have imagined it. Age made tricks of distance and shadow.

But standing alone in the lantern’s glow, wrapped in his father’s coat, letter ticking beneath the brass clock far below, Elias decided it did not matter whether he’d seen it or not.

He would light the lamp. He would let it go around, again and again, while strength remained.

Outside, the sea pressed close around the rock like an old, restless animal. In the tower, the old gear hummed softly, and the beam traced its long, unremarked circle through the night.

On the water, a captain glanced up from a glitching screen, frowning, and saw a thin, improbable shaft of light reaching through the fog, just where no chart said it should be.

He corrected his course by two degrees and did not crash on the reef that his grandfather had once feared.

By morning, he would forget the adjustment, chalk it up to experience. On another headland, a woman waiting at a kitchen window would see his ship’s lights appear on the horizon right when they ought to, and she would breathe easier, not knowing why.

The lighthouse keeper slept in his chair at the base of the tower, the coat pulled over him, the beam still turning above.

Light isn’t for the ships that know where they’re going, his younger hand had told him.

And so he kept it.
